title: Past simple: be and regular verbs
objectives: Describe finished past states using was and were.
Spell and use common regular past verb forms.
Form past simple questions and negatives.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Use the past simple to describe a finished situation or action in the past. ‘I was tired yesterday’ describes a past state. ‘We visited a museum last Saturday’ describes a completed action. Expressions such as yesterday, last week, last year and two days ago can show when it happened, but the time can also be clear from the conversation.

This unit introduces past forms of be and regular verbs. A regular verb usually forms its past with -ed: work becomes worked. The past form of be is different: it is was or were. You will study more irregular verbs in the next unit.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use was with I, he, she, it and a singular name or noun: ‘I was at home’ and ‘The shop was open’. Use were with you, we, they and plural nouns: ‘You were late’ and ‘The shops were open’. The form you were is used for one listener or several listeners.

For a negative with be, add not: was not or wasn’t; were not or weren’t. For a question, put was or were before the subject: ‘Was the film good?’ and ‘Were they at home?’ In a short answer, use was or were: ‘Yes, it was’ or ‘No, they weren’t’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: For most regular verbs, add -ed: work becomes worked and visit becomes visited. If the verb already ends in e, add -d: live becomes lived. If it ends in a consonant plus y, change y to i and add -ed: study becomes studied. Some short stressed verbs double the final consonant: stop becomes stopped. The spelling pattern depends on the word.

The past form of a regular verb is the same for every subject: I worked, she worked and they worked. To make a negative, use did not or didn’t plus the base verb: ‘She didn’t work’. For a question, put did before the subject and use the base verb: ‘Did she work?’ Use did or didn’t in a short answer.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Compare be and an ordinary verb: ‘Was he tired?’ but ‘Did he work?’ Do not use did with was in the same basic question: ‘Was he at home?’, not ‘Did he was at home?’ After did or didn’t, the main verb returns to its base form: ‘Did they visit?’, not ‘Did they visited?’

Regular past endings can sound different in speech. For example, worked, played and visited do not all end with the same sound, although each is written with -ed. In this unit, focus first on choosing the correct written form and on showing a completed past time.

examples.note: I takes was in the past.

examples.sentence: The children were tired after the trip.
examples.note: Children is plural and takes were.

examples.sentence: The café wasn’t open last night.
examples.note: Wasn’t is the negative form for a singular subject.

examples.sentence: Were you at school on Monday? Yes, I was.
examples.note: The question uses were with you; the answer uses was with I.

examples.sentence: We visited our friends last weekend.
examples.note: Visited is the regular past form of visit.
Study changes y to i before -ed.

examples.sentence: The bus stopped near the station.
Did she work on Friday? No, she didn’t.
examples.note: Did introduces the question and work stays in the base form.

common_errors.reason: Use the base form after didn’t.
Use the base form after did.

summary: Use was and were for past forms of be.
Form most regular past verbs with -ed, checking spelling changes.
Use did or didn’t with the base form of ordinary verbs in questions and negatives.
